chapter: Ch 4: Presentation and Disclosures Based Accounting Standards
unit: Unit 1: AS 1 Disclosure of Accounting Policies
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Introduction and Scope of AS 1
explain: Enterprises operate in diverse business environments, so a single rigid accounting policy cannot work for everyone.
Accounting standards frequently offer alternative treatments, leading to variations in reported figures even for identical transactions.
Diversity in accounting policies harms the comparability of financial statements across different entities.
AS 1 requires enterprises to disclose significant accounting policies so users can understand and compare financial statements properly.
This accounting standard applies mandatorily to all enterprises.

flow.title: Need for AS 1 Disclosures
steps: Enterprises operate in diverse business conditions

topics.example: If two retail businesses value unsold stock differently—one using FIFO and the other Weighted Average—users need to see the disclosed policy to make a fair comparison of their profits.
remember: AS 1 applies to all enterprises, without exception.
mistakes: Assuming AS 1 applies only to listed companies or corporate bodies.

quiz.q: To which of the following entities does AS 1 apply?
o: Only listed companies
Only manufacturing companies
All enterprises
Only entities with turnover exceeding ₹50 crores
quiz.why: AS 1 explicitly applies to all enterprises preparing financial statements.

quiz.q: What is the primary objective of disclosing accounting policies under AS 1?
o: To eliminate tax liability completely
To promote better understanding and comparability of financial statements
To replace the requirement of auditing books of accounts
To guarantee guaranteed dividend payout to shareholders
quiz.why: Disclosing accounting policies enables users to understand and compare financial statements of different entities meaningfully.

topics.title: Fundamental Accounting Assumptions
explain: AS 1 recognises three fundamental assumptions: Going Concern, Consistency, and Accrual.
Going Concern assumes an enterprise will continue operations in the foreseeable future without necessity or intent to curtail them.
Consistency means following the same accounting policies for similar transactions across periods to ensure comparability over time.
Accrual requires recording transactions when they happen, rather than when cash or cash equivalent is received or paid.
Section 128(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 makes it mandatory for companies to maintain accounts on an accrual basis.
If these fundamental assumptions are followed, no specific disclosure is required; disclosure is compulsory only if any assumption is NOT followed.

flow.title: Disclosure Test for Fundamental Assumptions
steps: Check Going Concern, Consistency, and Accrual
Verify if each assumption was followed
If followed, no disclosure is required
If not followed, disclose the fact

topics.example: A company records sales immediately when goods are delivered on credit instead of waiting for customer payment, and because accrual is routinely followed, no note mentioning this assumption is required.
remember: Specific disclosure is required only when a fundamental accounting assumption is NOT followed.
mistakes: Writing in exam answers that an enterprise must specifically state every year that it has followed going concern and accrual.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a fundamental accounting assumption under AS 1?
o: Going Concern
Consistency
Prudence
Accrual
quiz.why: Prudence is a major consideration for selecting accounting policies, not a fundamental accounting assumption.

quiz.q: When is an enterprise required to disclose a fundamental accounting assumption?
o: Every single financial year without fail
Only when the assumption is followed
Only when the assumption is NOT followed
Only when approved by the auditor
quiz.why: Fundamental assumptions are assumed to be followed; disclosure is needed only if they are not followed.

topics.title: Selection of Accounting Policies
topics.section: AS 1 & Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013
explain: Accounting policies are specific accounting principles and methods of applying them to prepare and present financial statements.
The primary goal of selecting accounting policies is to show a true and fair view of the enterprise's performance and state of affairs.
Prudence requires that profits are not anticipated, while all known liabilities and losses are provided for, avoiding overstatement of profits or understatement of losses.
Prudence does not permit the creation of hidden or secret reserves by deliberately overstating losses or understating assets.
Substance over form requires accounting for transactions based on their financial and economic reality, not merely their legal form.

Materiality requires disclosing all items that could influence user decisions, including quantitative limits specified under Schedule III (e.g., expenses exceeding 1% of revenue from operations or ₹1,00,000, whichever is higher, and shareholdings exceeding 5%).

flow.title: Criteria for Policy Selection
steps: Apply prudence to prevent profit overstatement
Prioritise economic substance over legal form
Ensure presentation gives true and fair view

topics.example: Valuing inventory at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower, reflects prudence by ignoring unrealised profits while recognising anticipated losses immediately.
remember: Major considerations in selection: Prudence, Substance over Form, and Materiality.
mistakes: Treating 'Comparability' as a primary criterion for policy selection; comparability is an objective, while prudence, substance over form, and materiality are the considerations.

quiz.q: Under AS 1, which of the following is a major consideration governing the selection of accounting policies?
o: Liquidity
Substance over form
Historical cost
Dual aspect
quiz.why: The three major considerations governing selection under AS 1 are Prudence, Substance over form, and Materiality.

quiz.q: According to Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013, an item of expense must be disclosed separately if it exceeds:
o: 5% of revenue or ₹50,000, whichever is lower
1% of revenue or ₹1,00,000, whichever is higher
2% of net profit or ₹2,00,000, whichever is higher
10% of total assets
quiz.why: Schedule III requires separate disclosure if an expense exceeds 1% of revenue from operations or ₹1,00,000, whichever is higher.

topics.title: Manner of Disclosure
explain: All significant accounting policies adopted by an enterprise must be disclosed as an integral part of the financial statements.
Disclosures should normally be presented at one central place rather than scattered across various statements, schedules, and notes.
Grouping policies together helps users review the accounting framework in an orderly and coherent manner.
topics.example: A company groups its depreciation method, inventory valuation policy, and revenue recognition policy into Note 1 of its annual report under the heading 'Significant Accounting Policies'.
remember: All significant accounting policies must be disclosed at one place as part of the financial statements.
mistakes: Scattering disclosures across several unrelated notes instead of placing them together in one place.

quiz.q: How should significant accounting policies be disclosed in the financial statements?
o: Scattered across individual asset and liability schedules
In the Directors' Report only
At one place as part of the financial statements
Only on the company's public website
quiz.why: Paras 18-20 of AS 1 require that disclosures form part of the financial statements and be placed together in one place.

quiz.q: Is disclosure of accounting policies a substitute for correct accounting treatment?
o: Yes, full disclosure cures wrong accounting treatments
No, disclosure cannot rectify an inappropriate accounting treatment
Yes, if approved by the board of directors
Yes, if stated in the notes to accounts
quiz.why: Disclosure of an incorrect or inappropriate accounting policy cannot rectify improper accounting.

topics.title: Disclosure of Changes in Accounting Policies
explain: An accounting policy may only be changed if required by statute, by an accounting standard, or for more appropriate presentation of financial statements.
Any change having a material effect in the current period must be disclosed, stating the ascertainable financial impact on statement items.
If the monetary effect of the change is not ascertainable wholly or in part, the enterprise must explicitly disclose that fact.
If a change has no material effect in the current year but is reasonably expected to have a material effect in later years, the fact must be disclosed in the period of adoption.

flow.title: Disclosure of Accounting Policy Changes
steps: If current material, disclose impact amount
If impact unascertainable, disclose that fact
If effect only in future, disclose fact now

topics.example: A company switches its inventory valuation from FIFO to Weighted Average, reducing current profit and closing inventory by ₹16,000; it must disclose both the switch and the ₹16,000 reduction.
remember: If a change will have material effects only in future periods, the fact of the change must still be disclosed in the current period.
mistakes: Deferring disclosure of a change to future periods when the financial effect actually emerges, rather than disclosing the fact in the year of adoption.

quiz.q: Under AS 1, when can an enterprise change an accounting policy?
o: Whenever management wishes to report higher profits
Only if required by statute, accounting standard, or for more appropriate presentation
Only after receiving approval from the Central Government
At the beginning of every financial year automatically
quiz.why: A policy can be changed only if required by statute, an accounting standard, or for more appropriate presentation.

quiz.q: If a policy change has no material effect in the current year but will have a material effect in future years, what must be done?
o: No disclosure is needed in any year
Disclose only in the future year when the effect arises
Disclose the fact of such change in the current period
Reverse the policy change immediately
quiz.why: AS 1 requires the fact of such a change to be appropriately disclosed in the period in which the change is adopted.
